tip: 'Om ... te' frames a purpose: 'om jullie te zien' means 'to see you'.
'Omdat' sends the verb to the end of its clause: 'omdat hij al laat is', with 'is' last.
'Pas' means not until, not 'soon': 'pas na het eten' is 'not until after dinner'.
'Thuis' means at home and needs no preposition; for going home you'd use 'naar huis': 'Meestal eet ik thuis'.
Dutch often fuses time words into one: 'morgenochtend' = 'morgen' + 'ochtend', tomorrow morning.
'Onze' is the possessive before 'de'-words and all plurals: 'onze excuses'.
'Wellicht' means perhaps and is more formal than the everyday 'misschien'.
'Beste' is the superlative of 'goed' ('goed', 'beter', 'best'): 'mijn beste vriend', my best friend.
Separable 'langskomen' (drop by) splits in the present: the prefix 'langs' moves to the end, 'komt hij langs'.
'Daarom' means that is why, or therefore; it points back to a reason to state its result.
'Fietsen' takes 'zijn', not 'hebben', in the perfect once a destination is named: 'is naar de winkel gefietst'.
Verbs of change of state take 'zijn' in the perfect: 'de temperatuur is gestegen', rose.
Many units of measure stay singular after a number: 'tien kilometer', not 'kilometers'.
'Terug-' (back) separates: 'terugkomen' → 'ik kom terug' (I come back).
'Over' plus a time span means 'in' that much time: 'over een uur' = in an hour.
'Enkel' here means only, like 'alleen'; it is common in Belgian Dutch: 'enkel op dinsdag'.
'Volgens mij' means in my opinion, literally 'according to me'; use 'volgens' plus a person.
'Hierna' means after this, something coming up; compare 'daarna', after that.
Dutch usually shows possession with 'van', not apostrophe-s: 'de fiets van mijn broer', my brother's bike.
You give something to someone with 'aan': 'ik geef de sleutel aan mijn buurman'.
'Hun' is the indirect-object pronoun, to them: 'de juf leest hun een verhaaltje voor'.
'Bedanken' takes 'voor' for the thing you thank someone for: 'bedankt haar voor de maaltijd'.
'Wegens' means because of, or due to, and takes a noun: 'geannuleerd wegens een storing'.
'Me' (unstressed) and 'mij' (stressed) both mean 'me': 'Geef me dat' vs 'Dat is voor mij'.
Dutch often uses 'op' for being at a workplace: 'op kantoor zijn', to be at the office.
Means of transport uses 'met': 'met de trein', by train; 'met de bus', 'met de fiets'.
Front a phrase and the verb stays second, ahead of the subject: 'Na de les gaan de studenten' (after the class go the students).
In the perfect a separable verb wraps 'ge-' inside: 'meenemen' becomes 'meegenomen' ('mee' + 'ge' + 'nomen').
'Elke' means every and is followed by a singular noun: 'elke dag', every day.
'Zodra' (as soon as) sends its verb to the end of the clause: 'zodra we het weten'.
